claim: Interferon (IFN) inhibits HIV replication by inducing antiviral effectors.
source: Interferon (IFN) inhibits HIV replication by inducing antiviral effectors.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about interferon's role in antiviral immunity.

claim: A modified lentiviral vector allows for packaging of sgRNA-encoding genomes in trans into budding HIV-1 particles.
source: we assembled a CRISPR sgRNA library of Interferon Stimulated Genes (ISGs) into a modified lentiviral vector that allows for packaging of sgRNA-encoding genomes in trans into budding HIV-1 particles.
evidence: The manuscript describes the creation and use of this modified vector system, with experimental data showing its function.

claim: Knockout of Zinc Antiviral Protein (ZAP) improved the performance of the screen due to ZAP-mediated inhibition of the vector.
source: We observed that knockout of Zinc Antiviral Protein (ZAP) improved the performance of the screen due to ZAP-mediated inhibition of the vector.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing improved correlation in screens performed in ZAP-KO cells (Figure 2C) and increased HIV-CRISPR packaging (Figure 2B).

claim: MxB, IFITM1, Tetherin/BST2 and TRIM5alpha together explain the inhibitory effects of IFN on the CXCR4-tropic HIV-1 strain, HIV-1LAI, in THP-1 cells.
source: A small panel of IFN-induced HIV restriction factors, including MxB, IFITM1, Tetherin/BST2 and TRIM5alpha together explain the inhibitory effects of IFN on the CXCR4-tropic HIV-1 strain, HIV-1LAI, in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PIKAHIV screen results (Figure 2E) and validation experiments showing reduced IFN inhibition in knockout cells (Figure 4B-C).

claim: A screen with a CCR5-tropic primary strain, HIV-1Q23.BG505, described an overlapping, but non-identical, panel of restriction factors.
source: A second screen with a CCR5-tropic primary strain, HIV-1Q23.BG505, described an overlapping, but non-identical, panel of restriction factors.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of screen results between HIV-1LAI and HIV-1Q23.BG505 shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The HIV-CRISPR screen identifies HIV dependency factors.
source: Further, this screen also identifies HIV dependency factors.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of depleted genes in the screen (Figure 5A) and validation of dependency factors like CXCR4, CD169, TLR2, and SEC62.

claim: IFN-induced restriction factors are incompletely antagonized by HIV strains in human cells.
source: The ability of IFN-induced restriction factors to inhibit HIV strains to replicate in human cells suggests that these human restriction factors are incompletely antagonized.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that IFN-induced restriction factors like TRIM5alpha and Tetherin still inhibit HIV despite the virus having evolved antagonism mechanisms.

claim: The HIV-1 pandemic resulted from a series of successive cross-species transmissions of primate lentiviruses.
source: The HIV-1 pandemic resulted from a series of successive cross-species transmissions of primate lentiviruses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sharp and Hahn, 2011.

claim: Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV) transmission from African Old World primates to chimpanzees yielded the recombinant virus SIVcpz, which ultimately crossed into humans.
source: Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV) transmission from African Old World primates to chimpanzees yielded the recombinant virus SIVcpz, which ultimately crossed into humans (Sharp and Hahn, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sharp and Hahn, 2011.

claim: Successful replication of lentiviruses in a new host species required adaptation to restriction factors in the new host.
source: Successful replication of lentiviruses in a new host species required adaptation to restriction factors in the new host (Etienne et al., 2015; Etienne et al., 2013; Kirmaier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Etienne et al., 2015; Etienne et al., 2013; Kirmaier et al., 2010.

claim: Restriction factors that target primate lentiviruses include TRIM5alpha, MxB, Tetherin, SAMHD1, the APOBEC3 family of cytidine deaminases.
source: Restriction factors that target primate lentiviruses include TRIM5alpha, MxB, Tetherin, SAMHD1, the APOBEC3 family of cytidine deaminases (Malim and Bieniasz, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malim and Bieniasz, 2012.

claim: Recently described restriction factors include SERINC3/5, Zinc Antiviral Protein (ZAP), GBP5, SLFN11, LGALS3BP (90K), and the HUSH complex.
source: more recently described factors such as SERINC3/5, Zinc Antiviral Protein (ZAP), GBP5, SLFN11, LGALS3BP (90K), the HUSH complex (Chougui et al., 2018; Krapp et al., 2016; Li et al., 2012; Lodermeyer et al., 2013; Rosa et al., 2015; Takata et al., 2017; Usami et al., 2015; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Nearly 200 other proposed restriction factors have been described.
source: as well as nearly 200 other proposed factors (reviewed in (Gélinas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Gélinas et al., 2018.

claim: HIV-1 has evolved accessory proteins that degrade many host restriction factors.
source: HIV-1 has evolved accessory proteins that degrade many host restriction factors (Duggal and Emerman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duggal and Emerman, 2012.

claim: Mutations preventing recognition by restriction factors represent a mechanism of escape from restriction.
source: Further, mutations preventing recognition by restriction factors, such as evolution of low CG dinucleotide content in the HIV-1 genome (Takata et al., 2017) or mutations in capsid (Kirmaier et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2013), represent another mechanism of escape.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takata et al., 2017; Kirmaier et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2013.

claim: Many restriction factors that target HIV-1 are induced by type I Interferon (IFN) and are therefore Interferon-Stimulated Genes (ISGs).
source: Many restriction factors that target HIV-1 are induced by type I Interferon (IFN) and are therefore Interferon-Stimulated Genes (ISGs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the relationship between IFN and restriction factors.

claim: Interferon has been implicated in at least partial control of HIV replication in chronically-infected individuals treated with IFN.
source: Interferon has been implicated in at least partial control of HIV replication in chronically-infected individuals treated with IFN (Asmuth et al., 2010; Azzoni et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asmuth et al., 2010; Azzoni et al., 2013.

claim: Interferon has been implicated in at least partial control of HIV replication in SIV-infected rhesus macaques.
source: as well as in SIV-infected rhesus macaques (Sandler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sandler et al., 2014.

claim: IFN levels have been correlated with higher viral load and decreased CD4 T cell counts in HIV-infected individuals.
source: In contrast, IFN levels have also been correlated with higher viral load and decreased CD4 T cell counts in HIV-infected individuals (Hardy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hardy et al., 2013.

claim: ISG expression exerts changing selective pressure on HIV evolution in vivo.
source: Further, it appears that ISG expression exerts changing selective pressure on HIV evolution in vivo since transmitted/founder (T/F) strains are relatively resistant to IFN compared to viruses isolated later in infection (Fenton-May et al., 2013; Iyer et al., 2017; Parrish et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fenton-May et al., 2013; Iyer et al., 2017; Parrish et al., 2013.

claim: Transmitted/founder (T/F) strains are relatively resistant to IFN compared to viruses isolated later in infection.
source: since transmitted/founder (T/F) strains are relatively resistant to IFN compared to viruses isolated later in infection (Fenton-May et al., 2013; Iyer et al., 2017; Parrish et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fenton-May et al., 2013; Iyer et al., 2017; Parrish et al., 2013.

claim: The HIV-1 LAI strain was isolated from a chronically-infected individual.
source: The HIV-1 LAI strain (HIV-1LAI) was isolated from a chronically-infected individual (Wain-Hobson et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wain-Hobson et al., 1991.

claim: HIV-1LAI is sensitive to type I IFN.
source: The HIV-1 LAI strain (HIV-1LAI) was isolated from a chronically-infected individual (Wain-Hobson et al., 1991) and is sensitive to type I IFN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing IFN inhibition of HIV-1LAI in THP-1 cells.

claim: Potent IFNα inhibition of HIV-1LAI can be observed in the THP-1 monocytic cell line.
source: Specifically, potent IFNα inhibition of HIV-1LAI can be observed in the THP-1 monocytic cell line (Goujon and Malim, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goujon and Malim, 2010.

claim: MxB was identified as an IFNα-induced factor in THP-1 cells.
source: MxB, an interferon-induced GTPase that binds to and blocks lentiviral capsids, was identified as an IFNα-induced factor in THP-1 cells (Goujon et al., 2013; Haller et al., 2015; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goujon et al., 2013; Haller et al., 2015; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: MxB is an interferon-induced GTPase that binds to and blocks lentiviral capsids.
source: MxB, an interferon-induced GTPase that binds to and blocks lentiviral capsids, was identified as an IFNα-induced factor in THP-1 cells (Goujon et al., 2013; Haller et al., 2015; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goujon et al., 2013; Haller et al., 2015; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: The role of MxB in the IFNα-induced inhibition of HIV infection in THP-1 cells has been questioned.
source: although the role of MxB in the IFNα-induced inhibition of HIV infection in these cells has been questioned (Opp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Opp et al., 2015.

claim: Restriction factors have previously been discovered through cDNA library screening or by comparing expression of transcript levels in permissive versus non-permissive cells.
source: Restriction factors have previously been discovered through cDNA library screening or by comparing expression of transcript levels in permissive versus non-permissive cells (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Neil et al., 2008; Sheehy et al., 2002; Stremlau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Neil et al., 2008; Sheehy et al., 2002; Stremlau et al., 2004.

claim: High-throughput approaches to find HIV restriction factors have focused on overexpression screens to identify broad antiviral ISGs.
source: More high-throughput approaches to find HIV restriction factors have focused on either overexpression screens to identify broad antiviral ISGs (Schoggins et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schoggins et al., 2011.

claim: High-throughput approaches to find HIV restriction factors have focused on overexpression screens to identify HIV-specific antiviral ISGs.
source: or HIV-specific antiviral ISGs (Kane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kane et al., 2016.

claim: A screen for HIV restriction factors was performed by transfection of siRNA pools.
source: Further, one screen for HIV restriction factors was also performed by transfection of siRNA pools (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: IFNα inhibits HIVLAI replication in THP-1 cells 10-fold.
source: IFNα inhibits HIVLAI replication in THP-1 cells 10-fold (Goujon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goujon et al., 2013.

claim: The HIV-CRISPR vector maintains complete HIV-1 LTR sequences on integration.
source: Thus, the HIV-CRISPR vector maintains complete HIV-1 LTR sequences on integration.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the vector construction and Figure 1A showing the LTR repair.

claim: Full-length HIV-CRISPR genomic RNA is produced after transcription from the LTR.
source: Importantly, in addition to internal promoters driving Cas9 and sgRNA transcription, full-length HIV-CRISPR genomic RNA is also produced after transcription from the LTR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the HIV-CRISPR vector with repaired LTR sequences.

claim: The PIKAHIV library contains 15,348 unique sgRNA sequences.
source: In total 15,348 unique sgRNA sequences were assembled into the HIV-CRISPR backbone to create the Packageable ISG Knockout Assembly or PIKAHIV library (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library composition.

claim: The PIKAHIV library targets 1905 ISGs.
source: For each of the 1905 ISGs present in our library, we selected a total of 8 sgRNA sequences from existing human whole-genome CRISPR/Cas9 libraries
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library composition.

claim: 200 Non-Targeting Control (NTC) sgRNA sequences that are not predicted to target any loci in the human genome were included in the PIKAHIV library.
source: 200 Non-Targeting Control (NTC) sgRNA sequences that are not predicted to target any loci in the human genome were also included (Shalem et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library composition with citation support.

claim: STAT1, IFNAR1, STAT2 and IRF9 were identified as the highest-scoring hits in the PIKAHIV screen.
source: We identified the type I IFN pathway genes, STAT1, IFNAR1, STAT2 and IRF9 as the highest-scoring hits (magenta in Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by the MAGeCK analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ZAP and its modifier TRIM25 were the next highest scoring hits after the IFN pathway genes.
source: After the IFN pathway genes, the Zinc Antiviral Protein (ZAP) and its modifier TRIM25 were the next to highest scoring hits.
evidence: This is supported by the MAGeCK analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ZAP is an antiviral effector that has potent activity against alphaviruses as well as moderate activity against retroviruses.
source: ZAP is an antiviral effector that has potent activity against alphaviruses as well as moderate activity against retroviruses (Bick et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2002; Kerns et al., 2008; Takata et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bick et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2002; Kerns et al., 2008; Takata et al., 2017.

claim: TRIM25 is a gene known to modify ZAP's antiviral activity.
source: TRIM25 is a gene known to modify ZAP's antiviral activity (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: ZAP blocks virus replication by degrading transcripts with a high CG dinucleotide content.
source: More recently, it was shown that ZAP blocks virus replication by degrading transcripts with a high CG dinucleotide content (Takata et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takata et al., 2017.

claim: N4BP1 is a poorly-characterized inhibitor of the E3 ligase ITCH in mice.
source: NEDD4 Binding Protein 1 (N4BP1), a poorly-characterized inhibitor of the E3 ligase ITCH in mice (Oberst et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oberst et al., 2007.

claim: N4BP1 has not been previously known for antiretroviral activity.
source: that has not been previously known for antiretroviral activity (Figure 1E; cyan).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding, supported by the screen results.

claim: N4BP1 encodes RNA binding domains and is proposed to have RNase activity.
source: N4BP1 encodes RNA binding domains and is proposed to have RNase activity (Anantharaman and Aravind, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anantharaman and Aravind, 2006.

claim: Knockout of ZAP only very modestly increased infection by HIV-1LAI.
source: Knockout of either gene only very modestly increased infection by HIV-1LAI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockout of N4BP1 only very modestly increased infection by HIV-1LAI.
source: Knockout of either gene only very modestly increased infection by HIV-1LAI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The HIV-CRISPR genome has high levels of CG dinucleotides, particularly in the Cas9 and Puromycin resistance ORFs.
source: Analysis of the CG dinucleotide content across the HIV-CRISPR genome shows high levels of CG dinucleotides, particularly in the Cas9 and Puromycin resistance ORFs, that are potential targets for ZAP-mediated RNA degradation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the sliding window analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ZAP KO allows for increased packaging of HIV-CRISPR genomes relative to wild type HIV-1LAI genomes in viral supernatants.
source: Indeed, we found enhanced packaging of HIV-CRISPR genomes relative to wild type HIV-1LAI genomes in the viral supernatant in cell clones with no ZAP expression (Figure 2B – 10.5% in wt THP-1 cells; 24.8% and 31.6% in the ZAP-KO clonal lines).
evidence: This is supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was better correlation in sgRNA representation across replicates performed in ZAP-KO THP-1 cells as compared to control THP-1 cells.
source: Indeed, there was better correlation in sgRNA representation across replicates performed in ZAP-KO THP-1 cells as compared to control THP-1 cells (Figure 2C; r2 = 0.92 and 0.94 for the ZAP-KO screens as compared to r2 = 0.87 for the screen in wild type THP-1 cells).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of ZAP-mediated inhibition from THP-1 cells improves performance of the HIV-CRISPR screen.
source: Therefore, deletion of ZAP-mediated inhibition from THP-1 cells improves performance of the HIV-CRISPR screen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the improved correlation and Gene Scores observed in ZAP-KO screens.

claim: Multiple genes, rather than a single ISG, are responsible for the IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV infection in THP-1 cells.
source: Therefore, multiple genes, rather than a single ISG, are responsible for the IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV infection in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that no single gene scored as highly as the IFN pathway genes.

claim: MxB, IFITM1, Tetherin, TRIM5alpha, UBE2L6, LGALS3BP/90K and SAMD9L are candidate restriction factors mediating the IFN inhibition of HIV-1 in THP-1 cells.
source: Further, a small subset of genes, including MxB, IFITM1, Tetherin, TRIM5alpha, UBE2L6, LGALS3BP/90K and SAMD9L, are candidate restriction factors mediating the IFN inhibition of HIV-1 in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MxB, IFITM1, Tetherin and TRIM5alpha are the most significantly-scoring hits in the PIKAHIV screen that are also highly-induced by IFN.
source: MxB, IFITM1, Tetherin and TRIM5alpha are the most significantly-scoring hits in the PIKAHIV screen that are also highly-induced by IFN (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MxB, IFITM1, Tetherin and TRIM5alpha have well-described anti-lentiviral functions.
source: All have well-described anti-lentiviral functions (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2011; Malim and Bieniasz, 2012; Neil et al., 2008; Stremlau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers.

claim: MxB plays a major role in the IFN block to infection in THP-1 cells.
source: Infection of MxB-KO cells confirms that MxB plays a major role in the IFN block to infection as there was rescue of the IFN effect as compared to controls (Figure 3B and C; the Fold Inhibition in MxB-KO cells is close to 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: MxB is a dominant, early-acting ISG inhibiting HIV replication in THP-1 cells.
source: Therefore, MxB is a dominant, early-acting ISG inhibiting HIV replication in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of IFN inhibition in MxB-KO cells.

claim: Viral entry is a key target of potent IFN-mediated restriction.
source: Viral entry is a key target of potent IFN-mediated restriction, specifically by ISGs such as IFITMs, a family of 5 membrane-resident antiviral genes in humans with broad antiviral effects (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shi et al., 2017 and established knowledge about IFITMs.

claim: IFITMs are a family of 5 membrane-resident antiviral genes in humans with broad antiviral effects.
source: specifically by ISGs such as IFITMs, a family of 5 membrane-resident antiviral genes in humans with broad antiviral effects (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shi et al., 2017.

claim: IFITMs restrict viruses that enter cells by fusion at the plasma membrane or in the endosome.
source: IFITMs restrict viruses that enter cells by fusion at the plasma membrane or in the endosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFITM function.

claim: Restriction of lentiviruses using distinct entry pathways are differentially affected by ISGs.
source: We hypothesized that sensitivity to MxB restriction may be dependent on the viral envelope since our previous work has shown that restriction of lentiviruses using distinct entry pathways are differentially affected by ISGs (Roesch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roesch et al., 2018.

claim: The IFN inhibition in the MxB-KO clonal lines is significantly lower than that of control clonal lines for VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1.
source: We found that while the IFN inhibition in the MxB-KO clonal lines is significantly lower than that of control clonal lines (Figure 3D; p = 0.014 unpaired t test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is still a large inhibition of replication of VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 by IFNα in MxB-KO cells.
source: there is still a large inhibition of replication of VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 by IFNα (Figure 3D; 53-Fold).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IFITM3 is the most significantly-scoring hit in the screen with VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1.
source: In contrast to the screen with wildtype virus, the antiviral proteins IFITM3 is the most significantly-scoring hit, along with IFITM1, IFITM2, TRIM5alpha and Tetherin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MxB ranks as hit #74 in the VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 screen.
source: MxB ranks as hit #74 in this screen (Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by the screen results.

claim: IFITMs are the dominant IFN-induced blocks to replication when HIV-1 is pseudotyped with the VSV-G envelope.
source: This suggests that IFITMs are the dominant IFN-induced blocks to replication when HIV-1 is pseudotyped with the VSV-G envelope.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results showing IFITM3 as the top hit.

claim: MxB does play a role in the IFN-mediated inhibition of VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 viruses.
source: However, these results show that while MxB does play a role in the IFN-mediated inhibition of VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 viruses (compare MxB-KO cells to NTCs in Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The effect of MxB is masked by dominant IFITM inhibition of VSV-G pseudotyped viruses.
source: this effect is masked by dominant IFITM inhibition of these VSV-G pseudotyped viruses (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results and validation experiments.

claim: Similar results showing IFITM dominance over MxB for VSV-G pseudotyped viruses have been reported recently elsewhere.
source: Similar results have been reported recently elsewhere (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: Viral entry route impacts restriction factor sensitivity.
source: Therefore, viral entry route impacts restriction factor sensitivity and the role of MxB in IFN inhibition of HIV-1 in THP-1s is partially-masked by other ISGs when HIV-1LAI is pseudotyped by VSV-G.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential results between wildtype and VSV-G pseudotyped virus screens.

claim: HIV-1 is thought to be highly-adapted to TRIM5alpha and Tetherin.
source: We were surprised to find TRIM5alpha and Tetherin in this screen as HIV-1 is thought to be highly-adapted to these human restriction factors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HIV-1 adaptation.

claim: IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV was significantly lower in MxB, TRIM5alpha and IFITM1 KO lines than in NTC pools.
source: while IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV was significantly lower in MxB, TRIM5alpha and IFITM1 KO lines than in NTCs pools (Figure 4B; MxB_1 = 2.6 fold, MxB_2 = 2.5 fold, TRIM5_1 = 3.9 fold, TRIM5_2 = 4.8 fold, IFITM1_1 = 4.7 fold, IFITM1_2 = 6 fold and IFITM1_3 = 4.3 fold in Figure 4C; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The largest rescue of IFN inhibition was observed in the MxB knockout pools.
source: The largest rescue we observed was in the MxB knockout pools (Figure 4C), confirming the key role of MxB in the IFN phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TRIM5alpha and IFITM1 contribute to IFNα inhibition of HIV-1LAI.
source: However, TRIM5alpha and IFITM1 also contribute to IFNα inhibition (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Tetherin KO has no effect on early steps of HIV replication.
source: We find no effect of Tetherin KO on early steps of HIV replication as expected given its role as a late-acting HIV restriction factor (Figure 4B; Tetherin_1 = 6 fold, Tetherin_2 = 6.4 fold in Figure 4C) (Neil et al., 2008; Van Damme et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C, and citations to Neil et al., 2008; Van Damme et al., 2008.

claim: There is a significant IFNα-mediated block to the late stages of the HIV lifecycle in both control and MxB-KO cells.
source: We also observed a significant IFNα-mediated block to the late stages of the HIV lifecycle (after translation of the viral Gag protein used to detect infection in Figure 4B) in both control and MxB-KO cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is still a 4.8-fold inhibition of virus released from MxB-KO clonal lines.
source: While MxB-KO clonal lines show a decreased IFN effect compared to NTC clonal lines (compare controls to MxB-KOs in Figure 4E), there is still a 4.8-fold inhibition of virus released from MxB-KO clonal lines (magenta in Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The HIV-1 Vpu accessory gene antagonizes Tetherin-mediated restriction.
source: The HIV-1 Vpu accessory gene antagonizes Tetherin-mediated restriction (Neil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neil et al., 2008.

claim: Deletion of Vpu sensitizes HIV-1 to Tetherin restriction.
source: Deletion of Vpu sensitizes HIV-1 to Tetherin restriction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Vpu function.

claim: Infection with Vpu-deficient HIV-1 in IFN-treated Tetherin-KO cells shows increased virus release as compared to control cells.
source: Infection with Vpu-deficient HIV-1 (HIV-1LAIΔvpu) in IFN-treated Tetherin-KO cells shows increased virus release as compared to control cells (Tetherin_1 = 20.5 fold, Tetherin_2 = 14 fold in Figure 4F – left panel), confirming the late inhibition of Vpu-deficient HIV by Tetherin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Infection of Tetherin-KO cells with wt HIV-1LAI shows significantly-increased virus release.
source: Infection of these cell pools with wt HIV-1LAI also shows significantly-increased virus release, suggesting that HIV-1LAI Vpu does not completely antagonize IFN-induced Tetherin in THP-1 cells (Tetherin_1 = 4.4 fold, Tetherin_2 = 2.14 fold in Figure 4F – right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: HIV-1LAI Vpu does not completely antagonize IFN-induced Tetherin in THP-1 cells.
source: suggesting that HIV-1LAI Vpu does not completely antagonize IFN-induced Tetherin in THP-1 cells (Tetherin_1 = 4.4 fold, Tetherin_2 = 2.14 fold in Figure 4F – right panel).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased virus release in Tetherin-KO cells.

claim: Tetherin is a late-acting ISG contributing to IFN inhibition of HIV-1LAI in THP-1 cells.
source: Therefore, Tetherin is a late-acting ISG contributing to IFN inhibition of HIV-1LAI in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased virus release in Tetherin-KO cells.

claim: The top hit in the dependency factor analysis is the HIV-1 co-receptor CXCR4.
source: The top hit is the HIV-1 co-receptor CXCR4 (Figure 5A) which is required for entry by HIV-1LAI
evidence: This is supported by the negative MAGeCK Gene Score analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CXCR4 is required for entry by HIV-1LAI.
source: The top hit is the HIV-1 co-receptor CXCR4 (Figure 5A) which is required for entry by HIV-1LAI
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1LAI entry requirements.

claim: SIGLEC1/CD169 is the next highest scoring hit in the dependency factor analysis.
source: The next highest scoring hit is SIGLEC1/CD169 (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by the negative MAGeCK Gene Score analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CD169 is an HIV attachment factor that has been characterized to facilitate trans infection of CD4 +T cells by DCs through binding to sialylated glycosphingolipids on the HIV particle.
source: SIGLEC1/CD169 (Figure 5A), an HIV attachment factor that has been characterized to facilitate trans infection of CD4 +T cells by DCs through binding to sialylated glycosphingolipids on the HIV particle (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012; Puryear et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012; Puryear et al., 2013.

claim: CD169 is upregulated by IFNα in THP-1 cells.
source: CD169 is upregulated by IFNα in THP-1 cells (Figure 5B – gray = untreated, purple =+IFN, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CD169 plays a role in cis-infection of monocytic cells.
source: Our screen only assays cell-autonomous effects suggesting that CD169 also plays a role in cis-infection of monocytic cells, consistent with recent work showing enhanced infection of THP-1 cells by CD169, specifically in the presence of IFNα (Akiyama et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results and supported by citation to Akiyama et al., 2017.

claim: CD169 knockdown cells are less susceptible to infection both in the presence and absence of IFN pretreatment.
source: Indeed, when CD169 expression is knocked-down (Figure 5B, right panel) these cells are less susceptible to infection both in the presence and absence of IFN pretreatment (Figure 5C), although this effect is stronger in presence of IFNα (6.5-fold vs 4.7-fold; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Siglec-1/CD169 is an IFN-induced, HIV dependency factor in THP-1 cells.
source: Thus, we find that Siglec-1/CD169 is an IFN-induced, HIV dependency factor in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results and validation experiments.

claim: TLR2 is a toll-like receptor characterized to recognize bacterial PAMPs.
source: TLR2, a toll-like receptor characterized to recognize bacterial PAMPs (Akira et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akira et al., 2006.

claim: TLR2 is a high-scoring hit in the dependency factor analysis.
source: TLR2, a toll-like receptor characterized to recognize bacterial PAMPs (Akira et al., 2006) is the next highest-scoring hit in our dependency factor analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the negative MAGeCK Gene Score analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Infection of TLR2-KO cells with wildtype HIV-1LAI demonstrates lower infection as compared to controls.
source: Infection of these cells with wildtype HIV-1LAI demonstrates lower infection as compared to the controls, although this effect is not as extreme as for CXCR4 KO (Figure 5E left panel; 31-fold decreased infection for CXCR4-KO lines in orange, 3-fold for TLR2-KO lines in green).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Infection of TLR2-KO cells with VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 shows a loss of infectivity similar to wild-type HIV-1.
source: Of note, infection with VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 shows a loss of infectivity similar to wild-type HIV-1 (Figure 5E bottom right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The effect of TLR2 on enhanced infection is independent of viral entry.
source: Therefore the effect of TLR2 on enhanced infection is independent of viral entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TLR2-KO affects both wildtype and VSV-G pseudotyped virus similarly.

claim: CXCR4-KO lines are efficiently infected by VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1.
source: Conversely, the CXCR4-KO lines are efficiently infected by VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 (orange in Figure 5E, right panel) as entry occurs independent of the CXCR4 co-receptor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SEC62 is a component of the protein translocation machinery in the ER membrane.
source: Finally, we investigated the effect of SEC62, on HIV replication. SEC62 is a component of the protein translocation machinery in the ER membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SEC62 function.

claim: Knockdown of SEC62 showed significant loss of expression.
source: Knockdown of SEC62 by transducing THP-1 cells with two lentiviral shRNA constructs targeting SEC62 showed significant loss of expression as measured by Western Blot (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Infection of SEC62 knockdown cells with wildtype HIV-1LAI showed decreased levels of infection.
source: Infection of these cells with wildtype HIV-1LAI showed decreased levels of infection (Figure 5G, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: SEC62 is a dependency factor for HIV replication in THP-1 cells.
source: Therefore, SEC62 is a dependency factor for HIV replication in THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing decreased infection in SEC62 knockdown cells.

claim: Infection of SEC62 knockdown cells via VSV-G pseudotyping demonstrates equivalent infection to control cells.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, infection via an alternative entry pathway via pseudotyping HIV-1 particles with VSV-G, demonstrates equivalent infection in control and SEC62 knockdown cells (Figure 5G, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Levels of CD4 on the cell surface are decreased in SEC62 knockdown cells.
source: Analysis of the cell surface expression of the HIV-1 receptor, CD4, shows that levels of CD4 on the cell surface are decreased in SEC62 knockdown cells (Figure 5H, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cell-surface expression of CXCR4 is not decreased in SEC62 knockdown cells.
source: Interestingly, we do not observe decreased cell-surface expression of CXCR4 (Figure 5H, right panel), suggesting that the effect of SEC62 knockdown on cell surface proteins is not global but specific to certain transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The effect of SEC62 knockdown on cell surface proteins is not global but specific to certain transmembrane proteins.
source: suggesting that the effect of SEC62 knockdown on cell surface proteins is not global but specific to certain transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on CD4 vs CXCR4 expression.

claim: The type I IFN pathway genes are the most significantly-scoring genes for HIV-1Q23.BG505.
source: Similar to our initial screening with HIV-1LAI the type I IFN pathway genes are the most significantly-scoring genes for HIV-1Q23.BG505 (Figure 6A and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MxB, TRIM5alpha, IFITM1 and UBE2L6 are among the top hits in the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen in common with HIV-1LAI.
source: We also find MxB, TRIM5alpha, IFITM1 and UBE2L6 to be among the top hits in this screen in common with HIV-1LAI (Figure 6A and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IFI16 is a cytoplasmic DNA sensor known to inhibit HIV.
source: We find IFI16, a cytoplasmic DNA sensor known to inhibit HIV (Jakobsen et al., 2013; Monroe et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jakobsen et al., 2013; Monroe et al., 2014.

claim: IFI16 is a restriction factor specific to HIV-1Q23.BG505.
source: We find IFI16, a cytoplasmic DNA sensor known to inhibit HIV (Jakobsen et al., 2013; Monroe et al., 2014), as a restriction factor specific to HIV-1Q23.BG505 (Figure 6B and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of screen results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tetherin is no longer a significantly scoring hit in the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen.
source: In contrast, Tetherin is no longer a significantly scoring hit in the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen (rank #1897/3812; Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that Tetherin plays less of a role in restriction of this primary isolate as compared to HIV-1LAI.
evidence: This is supported by the screen results.

claim: Tetherin plays less of a role in restriction of HIV-1Q23.BG505 as compared to HIV-1LAI.
source: suggesting that Tetherin plays less of a role in restriction of this primary isolate as compared to HIV-1LAI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results showing Tetherin is not a significant hit for HIV-1Q23.BG505.

claim: SLC35A2 and NFKB2 are highly-scoring genes for both HIV-1LAI and HIV-1Q23.BG505.
source: Finally, SLC35A2 and NFKB2, while not IFN-induced in THP-1s, are highly-scoring genes for both viruses (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of screen results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SLC35A2 is a nucleotide sugar transporter.
source: SLC35A2, a nucleotide sugar transporter (reviewed in Hadley et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Hadley et al., 2014.

claim: NFKB2 is a component of the NFKB transcription factor complex.
source: and NFKB2, a component of the NFKB transcription factor complex (reviewed in Vallabhapurapu and Karin, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Vallabhapurapu and Karin, 2009.

claim: SLC35A2 and NFKB2 may both negatively impact HIV replication in an IFN-independent manner.
source: may both negatively impact HIV replication in an IFN-independent manner.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that these genes score highly but are not IFN-induced.

claim: CCR5 is one of the most significantly-scoring depleted genes in the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen.
source: Similar to our HIV-1LAI screen we find the coreceptor (in this case CCR5) to be one of the most significantly-scoring depleted genes in the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the negative MAGeCK Gene Score analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SIGLEC1/CD169 is the highest hit in the HIV-1Q23.BG505 dependency factor screen.
source: SIGLEC1/CD169 is the highest hit in the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1) suggesting that this HIV attachment factor is important for infection also by a Clade A primary isolate.
evidence: This is supported by the negative MAGeCK Gene Score analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CD169 is important for infection by a Clade A primary isolate.
source: suggesting that this HIV attachment factor is important for infection also by a Clade A primary isolate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results.

claim: SEC62, TLR2, MYD88 and NFKB1 are important HIV dependency factors for HIV-1Q23.BG505.
source: In common with HIV-1LAI we also find SEC62, TLR2, MYD88 and NFKB1 again as important HIV dependency factors for HIV-1Q23.BG505 (Figure 6B and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of screen results.

claim: The role of SEC62 in CD4 receptor expression is supported by its identification as a hit for both HIV envelope-containing viruses but not for the VSV-G pseudotyped infection.
source: The role of SEC62 in CD4 receptor expression is further supported by our finding of SEC62 as a hit for both HIV envelope-containing viruses but not for the VSV-G pseudotyped infection (compare Figures 5A and 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of screen results across different viral entry routes.

claim: The IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV in THP-1 cells is due to the combined action of a small panel of ISGs.
source: We have designed and validated a novel CRISPR knockout screening approach in which the virus itself serves to report levels of infection to identify genes important for HIV infection. Subsequent deep sequencing can quantitate effects of individual gene knockouts on viral replication in a massively-parallel fashion. Using the PIKAHIV library targeting human ISGs, we demonstrate that the IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV in THP-1 cells is due to the combined action of a small panel of ISGs that includes known HIV restriction factors like MxB, TRIM5alpha, IFITM1 and Tetherin.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the screen results and validation experiments.

claim: Each of the ISGs MxB, TRIM5alpha, IFITM1 and Tetherin individually imposes only modest restriction of HIV replication but together mediate robust restriction.
source: Each of these ISGs individually imposes only modest restriction of HIV replication but together mediate robust restriction of HIV replication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the validation experiments showing partial rescue in individual knockouts.

claim: HIV is not able to completely antagonize or escape some host encoded restriction factors.
source: While HIV has evolved antagonism or evasion strategies for restriction factors that limit replication in cells from other species, the results here imply that HIV is not able to completely antagonize or escape some host encoded restriction factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that restriction factors still inhibit HIV despite known antagonism mechanisms.

claim: Incomplete antagonism of restriction factors may be due to conflicting evolutionary pressures acting on the HIV genome.
source: Such incomplete antagonism may be due to conflicting evolutionary pressures acting on the HIV genome.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary reasons for incomplete antagonism.

claim: HIV proteins must evade restriction factor recognition while maintaining other protein functions.
source: HIV proteins must evade restriction factor recognition while maintaining other protein functions, including evasion of other restriction factors and binding to required cellular host factors.
evidence: This is an inference about the constraints on HIV protein evolution.

claim: HIV is still partially-sensitive to human TRIM5alpha-mediated restriction.
source: Our finding of significant TRIM5alpha restriction in human cells suggests that HIV is still partially-sensitive to human TRIM5alpha-mediated restriction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screen results and validation experiments showing TRIM5alpha restriction.

claim: IFN-induced MxB restricts infection in THP-1 cells.
source: Similarly, we find that IFN-induced MxB restricts infection in THP-1 cells, consistent with previous work (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results, validation experiments, and citations to previous work.

claim: A signature of APOBEC3 G-to-A hypermutation in integrated proviruses can be observed in HIV-infected patients.
source: A similar example of incomplete antagonism of human restriction factors can be found in HIV-infected patients in which a signature of APOBEC3 G-to-A hypermutation in integrated proviruses can be observed (Cuevas et al., 2015; Sadler et al., 2010) despite the fact that HIV encodes an antagonist, Vif, that targets APOBEC3 proteins for degradation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cuevas et al., 2015; Sadler et al., 2010.

claim: HIV encodes an antagonist, Vif, that targets APOBEC3 proteins for degradation.
source: despite the fact that HIV encodes an antagonist, Vif, that targets APOBEC3 proteins for degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV Vif function.

claim: Both TRIM5alpha and Tetherin are rapidly-evolving genes in primates.
source: Both TRIM5alpha and Tetherin are rapidly-evolving genes in primates with described consequences for host adaptation by primate lentiviruses (Lim et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lim et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2005.

claim: Capsids from diverse primate lentiviruses have adapted to TRIM5alpha alleles in various primates.
source: Capsids from diverse primate lentiviruses have adapted to TRIM5alpha alleles in various primates and are variably-restricted by TRIM5alpha orthologs (Kirmaier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kirmaier et al., 2010.

claim: Selection for capsid mutations that evade TRIM5alpha restriction is a key adaptive step that HIV and related SIVs must make to successfully replicate in a particular primate species.
source: Selection for capsid mutations that evade TRIM5alpha restriction is a key adaptive step that HIV and related SIVs must make to successfully replicate in a particular primate species (Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2013.

claim: TRIM5alpha is active against HIV in Langerhans cells.
source: Consistent with a role for TRIM5alpha in humans, TRIM5alpha is active against HIV in Langerhans cells (Ribeiro et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ribeiro et al., 2016.

claim: TRIM5alpha polymorphisms are associated with the clinical course of HIV-1 infection.
source: and TRIM5alpha polymorphisms are associated with the clinical course of HIV-1 infection (van Manen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Manen et al., 2008.

claim: CA mutations in HIV-infected individuals have been associated with sensitivity to TRIM5alpha restriction.
source: Further, CA mutations in HIV-infected individuals have been associated with sensitivity to TRIM5alpha restriction (Battivelli et al., 2010; Onyango et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Battivelli et al., 2010; Onyango et al., 2010.

claim: Most studies of HIV have not been done in the context of IFN.
source: Also of note, most studies of HIV have not been done in the context of IFN despite evidence that TRIM5alpha is highly-IFN upregulated in HIV target cells (Carthagena et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field with citation support.

claim: TRIM5alpha is highly-IFN upregulated in HIV target cells.
source: despite evidence that TRIM5alpha is highly-IFN upregulated in HIV target cells (Carthagena et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carthagena et al., 2009.

claim: IFN-mediated TRIM5alpha inhibition of HIV represents a potentially-important role of TRIM5alpha particularly during acute infection when IFN levels are high.
source: Thus, our finding of IFN-mediated TRIM5alpha inhibition of HIV represents a potentially-important role of TRIM5alpha particularly during acute infection when IFN levels are high.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: More stable artificial variants of human TRIM5alpha can inhibit HIV-1.
source: More stable artificial variants of human TRIM5alpha can inhibit HIV-1 (Richardson et al., 2014), suggesting that increased TRIM5alpha levels, such as after IFN induction, may play a role in restricting HIV replication.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2014.

claim: Increased TRIM5alpha levels, such as after IFN induction, may play a role in restricting HIV replication.
source: suggesting that increased TRIM5alpha levels, such as after IFN induction, may play a role in restricting HIV replication.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation about artificial TRIM5alpha variants.

claim: Evasion of TRIM5alpha restriction may come at the cost of loss of fitness due to other requirements for capsid function.
source: Evasion of TRIM5alpha restriction may come at the cost of loss of fitness due to other requirements for capsid function within host cells such as uncoating, nuclear import and integration.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary constraints on HIV.

claim: Capsid sequences mediate evasion of other restriction factors, including MxB, or escape from host CTL responses.
source: Further, capsid sequences also mediate evasion of other restriction factors, including MxB, or escape from host CTL responses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about capsid function.

claim: Primary isolates of HIV-1 have increased sensitivity to TRIM5alpha that is proposed to be driven by CTL escape variants.
source: Primary isolates of HIV-1 have increased sensitivity to TRIM5alpha that is proposed to be driven by CTL escape variants (Battivelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Battivelli et al., 2011.

claim: Escape from IFITMs appears to be subject to conflicting evolutionary pressures.
source: Like TRIM5alpha, escape from IFITMs also appears to be subject to conflicting evolutionary pressures.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation about IFITM sensitivity evolution.

claim: IFITMs may exert significant selective pressure in vivo as HIV evolves increased susceptibility to IFITMs over the course of infection.
source: IFITMs may exert significant selective pressure in vivo as HIV evolves increased susceptibility to IFITMs over the course of infection (Foster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Foster et al., 2016.

claim: Further adaptation of HIV for efficient replication in human cells may not be possible due to constraints on viral evolution imposed simultaneously by multiple, independent restriction factor barriers.
source: In addition to basic required functions of HIV proteins, we further propose that further adaptation of HIV for efficient replication in human cells may not be possible due to constraints on viral evolution imposed simultaneously by multiple, independent restriction factor barriers.
evidence: This is speculation about the limits of HIV adaptation.

claim: MxB, TRIM5alpha, UBE2L6 and IFITM1 are strong hits in both the HIV-1LAI and the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screens.
source: MxB, TRIM5alpha, UBE2L6 and IFITM1 are strong hits in both the HIV-1LAI and the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screens (cyan in Figure 6B) suggesting that these ISGs inhibit a range of HIV isolates.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of screen results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: UBE2L6 has recently been shown to inhibit HIV in an overexpression assay and is antagonized by Vpu.
source: UBE2L6 has recently been shown to inhibit HIV in an overexpression assay and is antagonized by Vpu (Jain et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jain et al., 2018.

claim: LGALS3BP, SAMD9L and Tetherin/BST2 scored highly in the HIV-1LAI PIKAHIV screen but not the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen.
source: In contrast, several other ISGs scored highly in the HIV-1LAI PIKAHIV screen but not the HIV-1Q23.BG505 screen including LGALS3BP (also known as 90K or M2BP), SAMD9L and Tetherin/BST2 (dark blue in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of screen results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: UBE2L6 and 90K inhibit HIV in over-expression assays.
source: UBE2L6 and 90K inhibit HIV in over-expression assays (Jain et al., 2018; Lodermeyer et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jain et al., 2018; Lodermeyer et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016.

claim: SAMD9L was recently shown to be an IFN-induced restriction factor for poxviruses.
source: and SAMD9L was recently shown to be an IFN-induced restriction factor for poxviruses (Meng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meng et al., 2018.

claim: Tetherin/BST2, LGALS3BP/90K/M2BP and SAMD9L show differential, strain-dependent restriction.
source: Tetherin/BST2, LGALS3BP/90K/M2BP and SAMD9L therefore show differential, strain-dependent restriction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential screen results between HIV-1LAI and HIV-1Q23.BG505.

claim: IFI16 is a dsDNA sensor that has been implicated in sensing and inhibition of HIV infection.
source: IFI16 is a dsDNA sensor that has been implicated in sensing and inhibition of HIV infection (Jakobsen et al., 2013; Monroe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jakobsen et al., 2013; Monroe et al., 2014.

claim: IFI16 restricts HIV-1 in THP-1 cells in a strain-dependent manner.
source: Our results here suggest that IFI16 restricts HIV-1 in THP-1 cells in a strain-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IFI16 is a hit for HIV-1Q23.BG505 but not HIV-1LAI.

claim: Incomplete antagonism of Tetherin by Vpu may suggest a functional tradeoff.
source: Similar to TRIM5alpha, our finding of inhibition of wt HIV by Tetherin despite intact Vpu expression may suggest a functional tradeoff in which HIV Vpu is unable to completely antagonize host cell Tetherin activity.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for incomplete Tetherin antagonism.

claim: Primary HIV isolates better antagonize Tetherin as compared to HIV-1 NL4-3.
source: It has previously been shown that primary HIV isolates better antagonize Tetherin as compared to HIV-1 NL4-3 (Pickering et al., 2014) which may explain why Tetherin is a hit in the screen using HIV-1LAI, but not HIV-1 Q23.BG505.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pickering et al., 2014.

claim: Adaptation HIV-1 group M to the unique form of human Tetherin allele required evolution of the viral protein Vpu to antagonize Tetherin.
source: Adaptation HIV-1 group M to the unique form of human Tetherin allele required evolution of the viral protein Vpu to antagonize Tetherin (Kmiec et al., 2016; Lim et al., 2010; Sauter et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kmiec et al., 2016; Lim et al., 2010; Sauter et al., 2009.

claim: IFN treatment in HCV- and HIV- coinfected patients resulted in evolution of Vpu variants with stronger Tetherin antagonism.
source: Consistent with conflicting evolutionary constraints, IFN treatment in HCV- and HIV- coinfected patients resulted in evolution of Vpu variants with stronger Tetherin antagonism when ISGs are expressed in vivo (Pillai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pillai et al., 2012.

claim: More complete antagonism of Tetherin by Vpu might compromise some of the other functions of Vpu in cells.
source: Perhaps more complete antagonism of Tetherin by Vpu would compromise some of the other functions of Vpu in cells (Apps et al., 2016; Margottin et al., 1998; Schubert et al., 1998; Shah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations about other Vpu functions.

claim: A moderate level of Tetherin antagonism could be selected for if cell-to-cell transmission is enhanced by Tetherin restriction.
source: Further, a moderate level of Tetherin antagonism could be selected for if cell-to-cell transmission is enhanced by Tetherin restriction (Gummuluru et al., 2000; Jolly et al., 2010), such as is observed for MoMLV in mice (Liberatore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations about cell-to-cell transmission.

claim: Vpu counteracts UBE2L6.
source: Interestingly, Vpu counteracts UBE2L6 (Jain et al., 2018) which we describe as an inhibitor of both HIV-1LAI and HIV-1Q23.BG505 suggesting that Vpu from both viruses are unable to fully counteract UBE2L6 in IFN-treated THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jain et al., 2018.

claim: Vpu from both HIV-1LAI and HIV-1Q23.BG505 are unable to fully counteract UBE2L6 in IFN-treated THP-1 cells.
source: suggesting that Vpu from both viruses are unable to fully counteract UBE2L6 in IFN-treated THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that UBE2L6 is a hit for both viruses despite Vpu antagonism.

claim: ZAP mediates a small, but detectable inhibition of HIV replication.
source: We found that ZAP mediates a small, but detectable inhibition of HIV replication as we find enhanced infection of ZAP-KO cells both in the presence and absence of IFN pretreatment (Figure 2 - Supplemental Figure 1A and 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: N4BP1 has a modest effect on HIV replication both after IFN pretreatment and when constitutively-expressed.
source: Similar to the effect of ZAP, N4BP1 (Nedd4-binding protein 1) also has a modest effect on HIV replication both after IFN pretreatment and when constitutively-expressed (Figure 2 - Supplemental Figure 1C and 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The anti-lentiviral function of N4BP1 appears to be genetically linked to ZAP activity.
source: In our screen, the anti-lentiviral function of N4BP1 appears to be genetically linked to ZAP activity as N4BP1 is no longer a hit in the ZAP-KO screen (Figure 2 – Supplemental Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that N4BP1 is not a hit in ZAP-KO screens.

claim: N4BP1 may modify or enhance ZAP-mediated antiviral activity similar to TRIM25.
source: Therefore, N4BP1 may modify or enhance ZAP-mediated antiviral activity similar to the modification of ZAP activity described for TRIM25 (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the genetic linkage observed in the screen.

claim: N4BP1 does not play a role in ZAP-mediated inhibition of SFV.
source: However, we did not find a role for N4BP1 in ZAP-mediated inhibition of SFV (see Figure 2 – Supplemental Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The role of N4BP1 in ZAP's antiviral activity varies depending on the viral target.
source: Therefore, the role of N4BP1 in ZAP's antiviral activity varies depending on the viral target.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on HIV vs SFV.

claim: The HIV-CRISPR screening approach can simultaneously screen thousands of gene targets in a single experiment.
source: The HIV-CRISPR screening approach represents a significant advance in screening for host factors that affect HIV replication in several ways, including: (1) we can simultaneously screen thousands of gene targets in a single experiment
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the method.

claim: The HIV-CRISPR screening approach can use any virus strain.
source: (2) we can use any virus strain
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the method, demonstrated by screening with multiple HIV strains.

claim: The HIV-CRISPR screening approach does not need any type of reporter to assay infections as virus replication itself provides the assay readout.
source: (3) we do not need any type of reporter to assay infections as virus replication itself provides the assay readout
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the method.

claim: The HIV-CRISPR screening approach can capture host factors that affect all stages of the HIV life-cycle.
source: (4) we can capture host factors that affect all stages of the HIV life-cycle including entry, nuclear import, integration, transcription, nuclear export, translation, packaging, budding and release.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the method, supported by the identification of both early and late-acting factors.

claim: The screen is sensitive enough to find key factors in just a single round of viral replication.
source: Further the data presented here demonstrates that the screen is sensitive enough to find key factors in just a single round of viral replication, even when multiple factors together mediate potent inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the successful identification of restriction factors in a 3-day screen.

claim: SIGLEC1/CD169 plays a role in enhancing infection in THP-1 cells in cis.
source: We demonstrate that the HIV attachment factor, SIGLEC1/CD169, plays a role in enhancing infection in THP-1 cells in cis rather than the more fully described role of SIGLEC1 to mediate infection from dendritic cells to T cells in trans (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012; Puryear et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results and validation experiments showing CD169 as a dependency factor.

claim: TLR2 mediates enhanced infection of THP-1 cells by HIV-1 regardless of viral entry pathway used.
source: Further, we find that TLR2 mediates enhanced infection of THP-1 cells by HIV-1 regardless of viral entry pathway used, as it impacted infection through both the HIV envelope and the VSV-G glycoprotein (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Recent work in CD4 +T cells has demonstrated enhanced infection and/or viral production in T cells on stimulation of TLR2.
source: Recent work in CD4 +T cells has similarly demonstrated enhanced infection and/or viral production in T cells on stimulation of TLR2 (Bolduc et al., 2017; Ding and Chang, 2012; Ding et al., 2010; Equils et al., 2003; Henrick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers.

claim: MYD88 is a downstream effector for TLR2 activation of transcription.
source: Of note, MYD88, a downstream effector for TLR2 activation of transcription, is also a strong hit in our dependency factor screening (Figure 5A) suggesting that it is the downstream signaling functions of TLR2 that enhance infection.
evidence: This is supported by the screen results and established knowledge about TLR2 signaling.

claim: It is the downstream signaling functions of TLR2 that enhance infection.
source: suggesting that it is the downstream signaling functions of TLR2 that enhance infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MYD88 is also a hit.

claim: SEC62 is a novel HIV dependency factor that correlates with CD4 receptor cell surface expression.
source: In addition to CD169 and TLR2, our identification of SEC62 as a novel HIV dependency factor that correlates with CD4 receptor cell surface expression highlights the ability of the HIV-CRISPR screening approach to find genes that function in pathways (such as CD4 receptor expression) important for HIV infection.
evidence: This is supported by the screen results and validation experiments showing decreased CD4 expression in SEC62 knockdown cells.

claim: NFKB1 is a dependency factor.
source: Finally, as would be expected, NFKB1 is a dependency factor (Figure 5A) as it is a precursor to a downstream activator of the HIV LTR that is important for HIV infection
evidence: This is supported by the screen results and established knowledge about NFKB1 function.

claim: NFKB2 is a restriction factor in the screen.
source: although somewhat surprisingly NFKB2 is a restriction factor in the screen (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HIV-CRISPR screens have the capability of identifying pathways of both positive and negative HIV regulation.
source: Thus, HIV-CRISPR screens have the capability of identifying pathways of both positive and negative HIV regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identification of both restriction factors and dependency factors.

claim: A recent CRISPR knockout screen demonstrated that a pooled CRISPR approach to gene knockout could identify HIV dependency factors.
source: A recent CRISPR knockout screen demonstrated that a pooled CRISPR approach to gene knockout could identify HIV dependency factors (Park et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2017.

claim: The Park et al. study relied on Tat-driven LTR-GFP reporter gene expression and many rounds of spreading infection.
source: The screen by Park et al. relied on Tat-driven LTR-GFP reporter gene expression as well as many rounds of spreading infection across multiple weeks in culture in a T cell line.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the Park et al. study.

claim: PIKAHIV screening is performed over a single round of infection in three days.
source: In contrast, PIKAHIV screening is performed over a single round of infection in three days in the THP-1 monocytic cell line with the screen relying on virus replication itself to enrich for gene targets of interest rather than selecting on a reporter gene.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the PIKAHIV screening method.

claim: Park et al. screened with a whole-genome library while PIKAHIV screening was performed with an ISG-specific sgRNA library.
source: Further, Park et al screened with a whole-genome library while our screening has been performed with an ISG-specific sgRNA library (PIKAHIV).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of the two screening approaches.

claim: Park et al. specifically screened for HIV dependency factors while PIKAHIV screened with a specific focus on finding HIV restriction factors.
source: Moreover, we screened in the presence of IFN with a specific focus on finding HIV restriction factors, whereas Park et al. specifically screened for HIV dependency factors.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of the two screening approaches.

claim: Both the PIKAHIV screen and the Park et al. screen identify the appropriate HIV co-receptor.
source: Both screens do identify the appropriate HIV co-receptor (CXCR4 or CCR5 in our study and CCR5 in the Park et al. study).
evidence: This is a comparison of the results from both screens.

claim: 3 of the five genes identified by Park et al. (TPST2, SLC35B2 and CD4) are not represented in the PIKAHIV library.
source: Of note, 3 of the five genes identified by Park et al. (TPST2, SLC35B2 and CD4) are not represented in the PIKAHIV library and, therefore, could not be identified in our screen.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library composition.

claim: ALCAM is not found as a hit in the PIKAHIV screening.
source: The final gene identified by Park et al., ALCAM, is not found as a hit in our screening and may reflect important differences in cell type or other technical aspects of the screening approaches.
evidence: This is a comparison of the results from both screens.

claim: The genes identified by Park et al. are the HIV receptor or co-receptor, genes that affect CCR5 expression, or genes that affect the ability of cells to complex with other cells.
source: For example, the genes identified by Park et al. are the HIV receptor or co-receptor (CD4, CCR5), genes that affect CCR5 expression (TPST2 and SLC35B2) or genes that affect the ability of cells to complex with other cells (ALCAM).
evidence: This is an analysis of the types of genes identified in the Park et al. study.

claim: The Park et al. screen may reflect the loss of the ability of KO cells to support syncytia formation rather than a loss of HIV infection per se.
source: It is possible that the Park et al. screen may, therefore, reflect the loss of the ability of these KO cells to support syncytia formation rather than a loss of HIV infection per se.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the Park et al. results.

claim: Some hits identified in PIKAHIV screening were not found in the Park et al. study, including SEC62, TLR2 and SIGLEC1/CD169.
source: Some hits identified in our PIKAHIV screening were not found in the Park et al. study, including SEC62, TLR2 and SIGLEC1/CD169.
evidence: This is a comparison of the results from both screens.

claim: Differences in cell type, viral strains and screening approach likely explain differences between the PIKAHIV screen and the Park et al. study.
source: We hypothesize that differences in cell type, viral strains and screening approach likely explain these differences.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for differences between the two screens.

claim: The IFN inhibition of HIV-1 in a monocytic cell line is due the combined function of fewer than eight different genes.
source: In summary, here we describe a novel screen that is highly sensitive to detect restriction factors for HIV-1. This new tool shows that the IFN inhibition of HIV-1 in a monocytic cell line is due the combined function of fewer than eight different genes.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the screen results.

claim: IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV-1 in THP-1 cells is mediated by restriction factors for which HIV has described mechanisms of antagonism and/or escape.
source: Our results demonstrate that IFN-mediated inhibition of HIV-1 in THP-1 cells is mediated by restriction factors for which HIV has described mechanisms of antagonism and/or escape.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the identification of factors like TRIM5alpha, Tetherin, etc.

claim: The increased IFN sensitivity of specific HIV strains may be due to relaxation of constraints on the virus that would otherwise limit virus replication during transmission events.
source: The increased IFN sensitivity of specific HIV strains, such as those isolated during chronic HIV infection, may be due to relaxation of constraints on the virus that would otherwise limit virus replication during transmission events.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary dynamics of HIV.

claim: Conflicting functional constraints acting on HIV may result in incomplete antagonism or escape from host ISGs during chronic infection.
source: We propose that conflicting functional constraints acting on HIV may result in incomplete antagonism or escape from host ISGs during chronic infection.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary constraints on HIV.

claim: 1905 human ISGs were selected from gene expression datasets of type I IFN-stimulated cells.
source: 1905 human ISGs were selected from gene expression datasets of type I IFN-stimulated cells (Goujon et al., 2013; Hung et al., 2015; Linsley et al., 2014) or from previously assembled ISG overexpression (Schoggins et al., 2011) or shRNA libraries (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library construction with citation support.

claim: The PIKAHIV library is enriched in genes that are specifically expressed in HIV target cells.
source: Thus, the library is also enriched in genes that are specifically expressed in HIV target cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selection of ISGs from HIV-relevant cell types.

claim: The PIKAHIV plasmid library contains 15,339 of the 15,348 total sgRNAs included in the synthesis.
source: The PIKAHIV plasmid library was sequenced and contains 15,339 of the 15,348 total sgRNAs included in the synthesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library composition with reference to sequencing data.
